title: Indeterminate structures
summary: The organising idea is the split between force methods (unknowns are redundant FORCES) and displacement methods (unknowns are DISPLACEMENTS) — knowing which family a named method belongs to answers a surprising number of questions. Moment distribution is the most examined technique, and its two constants are the distribution factor (stiffness ratio at the joint) and the carry-over factor (½ to a fixed end, 0 to a hinge). Fixed end moments must be memorised; everything else in the method is arithmetic.

sections.heading: Degrees of indeterminacy
sections.body:
**Static indeterminacy D_s** is the number of unknown forces in excess of the available equilibrium equations; **kinematic indeterminacy D_k** is the number of unknown joint displacements.

**For a plane frame:**

> **D_s = 3m + r − 3j**  (m members, r reaction components, j joints)
> **D_k = 3j − r**, reduced by the number of members if **axial deformation is neglected**

Each **internal hinge** reduces D_s by one, because it supplies the extra equation **M = 0**.

**Standard values worth recognising immediately:**

| Structure | D_s |
|---|---|
| Simply supported beam | **0** — determinate |
| Cantilever | **0** |
| **Propped cantilever** | **1** |
| **Fixed beam** | **2** (3 if axial force counted) |
| **Continuous beam, n spans** | **n − 1** |
| **Two-hinged arch** | **1** |
| **Fixed arch** | **3** |
| **Three-hinged arch** | **0** — determinate |
| Single-bay single-storey portal, fixed feet | **3** |
| Single-bay portal, hinged feet | 1 |

**Why indeterminacy is usually desirable** — and this comparison is examined directly:

| Indeterminate structure | Determinate structure |
|---|---|
| **Redundancy** — alternative load paths, so one member's failure need not mean collapse | Failure of one member causes collapse |
| **Smaller moments and deflections** for the same span and load | Larger |
| **Load redistribution** after local yielding | None |
| **Sensitive to support settlement, temperature change and fabrication error** | **Unaffected** by all three |
| More material-efficient | Simpler to analyse and build |

The fourth row is the price paid. A determinate structure simply **moves** when a support settles, developing no stress; an indeterminate one is **restrained**, so settlement, temperature change and shrinkage all induce genuine **secondary stresses**. That is why a three-hinged arch is chosen where foundations are uncertain, why long bridges have expansion joints, and why a continuous beam on soft ground must be checked for differential settlement.

**The two families of method** — knowing which is which answers many questions on its own:

| Family | Unknowns | Methods |
|---|---|---|
| **Force (flexibility) methods** | **Redundant FORCES** | Consistent deformation, **three-moment equation**, **strain energy / least work**, column analogy |
| **Displacement (stiffness) methods** | **Joint DISPLACEMENTS** | **Slope-deflection**, **moment distribution**, **Kani's method**, **matrix stiffness / finite element** |

**Force methods** are efficient when D_s is small (a propped cantilever, a two-hinged arch); **displacement methods** when D_k is small relative to D_s (a multi-storey frame with many redundants but few joint rotations). The **matrix stiffness method** dominates modern practice because it is systematic and mechanisable, which is precisely the displacement family's advantage.

sections.heading: Force methods
sections.body:
**Method of consistent deformation (the general force method):**

1. Choose **redundants** and remove them to leave a **determinate released structure**.
2. Compute the displacement of the released structure under the **applied loads** — call it Δ₀.
3. Compute the displacement due to a **unit value** of each redundant — the **flexibility coefficients** δ_ij.
4. Write **compatibility**: the total displacement at each released point must equal its actual value (usually zero).
5. Solve for the redundants, then find all forces by statics.

> **Δ₀ + Σ δ_ij R_j = 0**

The flexibility matrix **[δ] is symmetric**, by Maxwell's reciprocal theorem — which is a useful check on any hand computation.

**A worked case in outline.** For a **propped cantilever** with a UDL, remove the prop as the redundant. The free-end deflection under the UDL is wL⁴/8EI downward; that due to a unit upward prop force is L³/3EI. Compatibility (zero deflection at the prop) gives

> R = (wL⁴/8EI)/(L³/3EI) = **3wL/8**

and the fixed-end moment follows as **wL²/8**. The whole method is contained in that example.

**Clapeyron's theorem of three moments** — the specialised force method for **continuous beams**:

> **M₁L₁ + 2M₂(L₁ + L₂) + M₃L₂ = −6(A₁x̄₁/L₁ + A₂x̄₂/L₂)**

for spans of equal EI on level supports, where A x̄ are the moment-area terms of the simply supported moment diagrams. Written for each pair of adjacent spans, it gives as many equations as unknown support moments.

With **unequal EI** the terms are divided by I, and with **support settlement** an extra term **6E(δ₁/L₁ + δ₂/L₂)** appears — which is exactly how settlement induces moments in a continuous beam, and a standard examination extension.

**Strain energy method (theorem of least work).** For an indeterminate structure the redundants take the values that **minimise the total strain energy**:

> **∂U/∂R = 0** for each redundant R

This is Castigliano's second theorem, and it gives the same equations as consistent deformation — which it must, since both express compatibility.

**Two-hinged arch** is the classic application. Taking the horizontal thrust H as the redundant and minimising strain energy:

> **H = ∫(M y ds/EI) / ∫(y² ds/EI)**

where M is the moment of the equivalent simply supported beam. Corrections for **rib shortening**, **temperature change** and **abutment yield** are then added — each reducing or increasing H, and each absent from a three-hinged arch.

sections.heading: Slope-deflection and moment distribution
sections.body:
**Fixed end moments** must be memorised, because both methods start from them:

| Loading on a span L | FEM at each end |
|---|---|
| **UDL w over the whole span** | **wL²/12** |
| **Central point load W** | **WL/8** |
| Point load W at a from left, b from right | **Wab²/L²** and **Wa²b/L²** |
| Triangular, zero at one end, peak w at the other | wL²/30 and wL²/20 |
| Couple M at mid-span | M/4 |
| **Support settlement δ (one end)** | **6EIδ/L²** |

For a span with the **far end hinged**, the FEM is modified: a UDL gives **wL²/8** at the fixed end and zero at the hinge.

**Slope-deflection method.** For a member AB:

> **M_AB = (2EI/L)(2θ_A + θ_B − 3Δ/L) + FEM_AB**
> **M_BA = (2EI/L)(2θ_B + θ_A − 3Δ/L) + FEM_BA**

The unknowns are the **joint rotations θ** and the **sway Δ**. Equations come from **joint equilibrium** (ΣM = 0 at each joint) plus, where sway is possible, a **shear (sway) equation** for each storey.

It is systematic and handles sway naturally, but the number of simultaneous equations grows quickly — which is what motivated moment distribution.

**Moment distribution (Hardy Cross) — the most examined technique in the subchapter.** It is an **iterative** displacement method that avoids simultaneous equations entirely.

**The two constants:**

> **Distribution factor DF = (I/L) of the member ÷ Σ(I/L) of all members at the joint**
> **Carry-over factor: ½ to a FIXED far end, 0 to a HINGED far end**

The distribution factors at any joint must **sum to 1** — the first arithmetic check to make.

**Relative stiffness** is **I/L** for a member fixed at the far end, but **¾(I/L)** for one **hinged** at the far end. Using the reduced stiffness for the hinged member lets the hinge be dealt with once at the start rather than balanced repeatedly, which shortens the work considerably.

**The procedure:**

1. Compute all **fixed end moments**, treating every joint as locked.
2. At each joint, find the **out-of-balance moment** (the algebraic sum of the FEMs) and **distribute its negative** among the members in proportion to their DFs.
3. **Carry over half** of each distributed moment to the far end.
4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until the carry-overs are negligibly small.
5. **Sum each column** to get the final moments.

The method converges because each cycle's corrections are smaller than the last — typically three or four cycles suffice for engineering accuracy.

**Sway.** For a frame that can sway, moment distribution is done in two stages: a **non-sway** analysis with the frame artificially held, then a **sway** analysis with an arbitrary sway moment, and the two combined so that the **net storey shear is zero**. This is where the method becomes laborious, and where **Kani's method** (which builds the sway correction into the iteration) or matrix analysis is preferred.

**Its lasting value** is conceptual as much as computational: moment distribution makes visible **how a joint shares moment according to member stiffness**, which is the single most useful intuition in frame behaviour. A designer who understands it can predict where moments will go when a member size is changed.

sections.heading: Matrix methods, portal frames and plastic analysis
sections.body:
**The matrix stiffness method** generalises the displacement approach:

> **[K]{D} = {F}**

Member stiffness matrices are formed in local coordinates, **transformed** to global axes, and **assembled** into a global stiffness matrix by adding the contributions at shared degrees of freedom. Boundary conditions are applied by eliminating or penalising the restrained degrees of freedom, and the equations solved for the displacements; member forces then follow from the local stiffness relations.

**Properties of the global stiffness matrix:**

| Property | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Symmetric** | By Maxwell's reciprocal theorem — halves the storage and provides a check |
| **Banded / sparse** | Efficient solution; node numbering affects the bandwidth |
| **Positive definite** after boundary conditions | A unique solution exists |
| **Singular** before boundary conditions | Because the free structure can translate and rotate |

That last point is worth understanding: an unrestrained structure has **rigid body modes**, so its stiffness matrix has no inverse. A singular matrix in practice therefore signals a **missing restraint or a mechanism** — the commonest error message in structural software, and one whose meaning follows directly from the theory.

The **flexibility method** has a matrix form too, **[f]{F} = {D}**, but the stiffness method dominates because assembling stiffness contributions is a purely local, automatable operation while choosing redundants is not.

**Approximate methods for lateral load on frames** remain useful for checking software output and for preliminary design:

| Method | Assumption | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Portal method** | **Shear** distributed among columns; interior columns take **twice** the shear of exterior ones; hinges at member mid-points | **Low-rise, wide** frames |
| **Cantilever method** | **Axial force** in columns proportional to distance from the centroid, as in a cantilever beam | **Tall, slender** frames |
| Substitute frame | An isolated portion analysed with assumed end conditions | Gravity load on a multi-storey frame |

The **portal versus cantilever** choice reflects which action dominates: a squat frame resists lateral load mainly by **frame shear**, a tall one mainly by **overall bending**, with the columns acting like the flanges of a giant cantilever.

**Plastic analysis** — a different philosophy, and increasingly examined:

> **Plastic moment M_p = f_y Z_p**, where **Z_p** is the plastic section modulus
> **Shape factor = Z_p/Z_e**

| Section | Shape factor |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle** | **1.5** |
| **Circle** | **1.7** |
| **I-section** | **1.10 – 1.20** |
| Diamond | 2.0 |

The **I-section's low shape factor** is because it is already near-optimal elastically — little reserve remains between first yield and full plasticity. A rectangle, with much material near the neutral axis doing little elastically, has far more to give.

**Collapse occurs when enough plastic hinges form to create a mechanism:**

> **Number of hinges for collapse = D_s + 1**

So a simply supported beam (D_s = 0) needs **one** hinge, a propped cantilever **two**, and a fixed beam **three**.

**Collapse loads** for a fixed beam under UDL: **w_c = 16 M_p/L²**, against the elastic limit of 12 M_p/L² — a **33% reserve** beyond first yield, arising entirely from **moment redistribution** as successive hinges form. That reserve is what plastic design exploits and what elastic design leaves unused.

**The three theorems** of plastic analysis:

| Theorem | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Lower bound (static)** | Any load for which a **safe, statically admissible** moment distribution exists is **≤ the collapse load** |
| **Upper bound (kinematic)** | Any load computed from an **assumed mechanism** is **≥ the collapse load** |
| **Uniqueness** | The load satisfying both is **the** collapse load |

The practical method follows from the upper bound theorem: **try every plausible mechanism and take the lowest collapse load**, because the true value cannot exceed the smallest upper bound. For a portal frame the candidates are the **beam mechanism**, the **sway mechanism** and the **combined mechanism**.

**The requirement for plastic design** is **ductility**: only a **plastic (Class 1)** section, as defined by IS 800:2007's width-to-thickness limits, can form and sustain a plastic hinge through the rotation the mechanism demands. A **slender** section buckles locally before reaching M_p, so no redistribution is possible and plastic analysis is invalid. That is why section classification precedes any plastic calculation.

formulas.label: Degrees of indeterminacy
formulas.expression: plane frame D_s = 3m + r − 3j ;   D_k = 3j − r (less m if axial deformation ignored)
formulas.note: Each internal hinge reduces D_s by one, supplying the equation M = 0.

formulas.label: Consistent deformation (force method)
formulas.note: The flexibility matrix is symmetric, by Maxwell's reciprocal theorem.

formulas.label: Three-moment equation (Clapeyron)
formulas.note: Support settlement adds 6E(δ₁/L₁ + δ₂/L₂) — the mechanism by which settlement induces moments.

formulas.label: Fixed end moments
formulas.expression: UDL wL²/12 ;  central point load WL/8 ;  eccentric Wab²/L² and Wa²b/L² ;  settlement 6EIδ/L²
formulas.note: With the far end HINGED, a UDL gives wL²/8 at the fixed end and zero at the hinge.

formulas.label: Slope-deflection equation
formulas.note: Unknowns are joint rotations and sway; equations from joint equilibrium plus a sway equation per storey.

formulas.label: Moment distribution constants
formulas.expression: DF = (I/L)/Σ(I/L) at the joint ;   carry-over = ½ to a fixed end, 0 to a hinge
formulas.note: DFs at a joint must sum to 1. Relative stiffness is ¾(I/L) for a member hinged at the far end.

formulas.label: Two-hinged arch thrust (strain energy)
formulas.note: Then corrected for rib shortening, temperature and abutment yield — all absent in a three-hinged arch.

formulas.label: Matrix stiffness method
formulas.note: K is symmetric and banded; singular before boundary conditions, because of rigid body modes.

formulas.label: Plastic moment and shape factor
formulas.expression: M_p = f_y Z_p ;   shape factor = Z_p/Z_e     (rectangle 1.5, circle 1.7, I-section 1.10–1.20)
formulas.note: Requires a PLASTIC (Class 1) section; a slender section buckles before reaching M_p.

formulas.label: Plastic collapse
formulas.expression: hinges for collapse = D_s + 1 ;   fixed beam under UDL: w_c = 16 M_p/L²
formulas.note: A 33% reserve over the elastic limit of 12M_p/L², from moment redistribution.
